Manufacturing
Reporting period: 1 September 2025 - 16 October 2026
Geography: global, primary focus EU, EEA and UK; North American and East Asian evidence comparative
Migrated edition - evidence as of 16 October 2026; no research update
Classification: not specified in source edition (external public data only)
legacy: Report header: boundary; no classification in source edition

elements.visible_text: Version 1.0-M (migrated from the 16 October 2026 baseline) - Status: NEEDS_REVIEW, not a v4 edition
Audience: Senior Credit Officers; inherent sector exposure, not a borrower assessment.

slides.label: Executive Sector Risk Snapshot
slides.headline: Cyber/ICT and operational-resilience exposure is provisionally High, driven by IT-dependent production and supplier cascades; fraud and governance are not assessable.

ratings.just: No fraud research (Q10); the source edition covers cyber incidents and their outcomes only.
Manufacturing held 25.2% of EU ransomware claims in 2025 and about 65% of industrial ransomware in Q2 2026; four of five named incidents stopped production through IT.
One OEM stop was modelled to affect over 5,000 UK organisations; supplier prepayment and a GBP 1.5 billion state-guaranteed loan followed.
Fragments only (NIS2 management-body accountability; MOD supplier flow-down); no governance research (Q13).

elements.visible_text: Key messages: (1) production stops when enterprise IT stops, not mainly through plant control systems; (2) one OEM stop cascades to thousands of suppliers; (3) losses arrive through lost output and cash, not response cost.
Threat direction: rising in claim-based data (European manufacturing ransomware victims up 85.4% in January-July 2026 year on year); no prior edition exists for a trend comparison.

Most consequential credit implication: a multi-week stop at a large manufacturer drains cash (JLR free cash outflow of GBP 1.5 billion in one quarter, mixed causes) and transfers liquidity stress to suppliers.
Provisional: no approved rubric and no 24-sector calibration; ratings are migrated analytical judgements with confidence capped at Medium, not borrower assessments.
Sources: S-001, S-004, S-006, S-009, S-041, S-045, S-049, S-081 (Tier 1); S-010, S-039, S-040 (Tier 2) - Period: Sep 2025 - Oct 2026; 2025 benchmarks - Cut-off 16 Oct 2026 - v1.0-M Migrated

slides.label: Sector Anatomy: Key Operations & Dependencies
slides.headline: Manufacturing output depends on the enterprise systems that release production and on just-in-time supplier tiers; one OEM or one shared tool can stop many firms at once.

elements.visible_text: Footprint: about 2.2 million EU manufacturing enterprises in 2023, with machinery, food and motor vehicles the largest divisions by value added; JLR employs 34,000 people in the UK.
Plant control systems can be intact while production stops: JLR, Asahi, Stryker and Boston Scientific halted or slowed plants after IT shutdowns or outages.
Ask whether a borrower can release production and ship without ERP, MES and identity services, and which single customer or supplier accounts for most of its revenue.
Market shares of ERP, MES and OT vendors are not public, so no platform is described as dominant. Not covered in source edition: operating-model and governance complexity (Q13).

slides.label: Cyber Threat Landscape & Attack Scenarios
slides.headline: Ransomware against enterprise IT and misuse of administrative tools carry the highest disclosed production impact; exposed OT products and providers spread it across customers.

headers: Pathway (pattern, not an attack) and mechanism
rows: P1 Ransomware and data extortion against enterprise IT (targeted disruption)
JLR and Asahi, Sep 2025; Boston Scientific, Aug 2026; 25.2% of EU ransomware claims in 2025
P2 Destructive misuse of administrative platforms (common dependency)
Stryker, Mar 2026 (mechanism media-reported); CISA endpoint-management alert
P3 Internet-exposed OT and fielded products (supply-chain concentration)
Numerous refrigeration-controller compromises, Oct 2026; US PLC advisory, Apr 2026
P4 Supplier and service-provider compromise (supply-chain concentration)
Egide via an IT provider, Oct 2026; 117 ICS-ecosystem incidents in Q2 2026
P5 Data theft, intellectual-property and export-control exposure (other)
Asahi up to about 1.9 million records; West Pharmaceutical exfiltration, May 2026

elements.visible_text: Last 12 months: five named incidents; industrial ransomware rose 12% from Q1 to Q2 2026, with manufacturing about 65%. Last 30 days before cut-off: Egide site interruption (6-9 October 2026) and refrigeration-controller compromises (12-13 October 2026).
Dragos found no Q2 2026 ransomware case reaching control-system manipulation; disruption came from losing the enterprise and virtualisation layers that OT depends on.
Weight borrower discussions toward IT-OT production dependency, control of administrative tools and the exposure of products already sold, not ransomware claim counts.

Ranking and impact levels are migrated judgements, not measured outcomes; claim counts measure visibility, not attack rates. Not covered in source edition: developments after the 16 October 2026 cut-off.

slides.label: Geopolitical Cyber Threat Outlook
slides.headline: State-linked activity is a rising threat to industrial controllers and enterprise estates, but no official source in the period attributed a manufacturing disruption to a state actor.
lanes: US joint advisory on Iranian-affiliated actors exploiting internet-facing PLCs, Apr 2026
Makers and industrial users of the same controllers
Government advisory; manufacturing not a named sector
Destructive activity claimed by a state-linked persona
Claim unconfirmed; no US government attribution
NCSC: most nationally significant UK incidents originate directly or indirectly from nation states
Revised EU investment-screening regulation published 26 Jun 2026; UK NSI Act covers 17 areas

elements.visible_text: Unconfirmed claims: a criminal group's claim for JLR was not confirmed by the company or the NCA; ENISA recorded more unconfirmed hacktivist intrusion claims against manufacturing OT in 2025.
Defence, medical-device and OT-vendor manufacturers face added intent: US defence certification gates have applied since 10 November 2025 and controller fleets are reachable online.
Treat state-linked activity as a monitoring trigger rather than a rating driver; ask defence and OT-vendor borrowers about certification status and installed-base exposure.
Not covered in source edition: dedicated geopolitical analysis (Q07), exposed-region mapping and espionage against manufacturers; evidence is US-centred and official attribution is absent.

slides.label: Major Cyber Incidents & Lessons Learned
slides.headline: Five named incidents meet the evidence standard; four stopped production through IT, and the JLR case shows the path from shutdown to supplier liquidity and state support.
timeline: Jaguar Land Rover - automotive, UK and Slovakia
Enterprise systems shut down proactively; access route not disclosed
About five weeks of halted production; GBP 260 million cyber costs over two quarters
Supplier liquidity needs a bridge (case study)
Asahi Group - beverages and food, Japan
Data-centre network entered via network equipment at a group site
Shipments halted; about JPY 40 billion 2025 impact; results delayed five months
Global IT disruption; device wipe media-reported
Material Q1 effect; manufacturing and ordering restored in about four weeks
One administrative plane reaches every site
Unauthorised activity in IT systems; network outage
Manufacturing, ordering and shipping disrupted; guidance unlikely to be met
Numerous compromises; hundreds of stores affected; cost not disclosed

elements.visible_text: Selection: in-period event or outcome, Tier 1 support, manufacturing subsector and a distinct lesson. Considered but not selected: West Pharmaceutical, Egide, Hasbro and RTX.
Disclosure is asymmetric: two of five cases come from US securities filings and one from a Japanese company; only JLR and the controller case are EU or UK.
Treat a multi-week stop at a large OEM as a foreseeable credit event for its supplier base; ask how a borrower would bridge a key customer's stop.

Not covered in source edition: the second and third detailed case studies (only JLR is reconstructed) and developments after 16 October 2026; JLR's access route, OT state and full-year cyber cost were not disclosed.
legacy: Ch5 what the case does not establish

slides.label: Control Weaknesses & Resilience Priorities
slides.headline: Seven resilience priorities follow the observed attacks; production release without IT, control of administrative tools and supplier liquidity address the highest-impact pathways.

rows: A1 Production depends on ERP, MES and identity
A2 Administrative tools can wipe every device
A3 Suppliers depend on one customer
A6 New product reporting and liability duties

elements.visible_text: Capabilities that contain disruption in the source edition: offline production release, segmentation (Stryker restored in about four weeks), buffered inventory, multi-sourcing and supported firmware.
Labelled cyber costs were small beside lost output and cash, so continuity capabilities carry the cash-flow weight.
Use the priorities as discussion topics with borrowers; they are not a control audit or a compliance finding.
Priorities are sector-informed; scenario links and confidence are migrated judgements; no control-effectiveness data exists for any firm.

elements.visible_text: Status at cut-off: German NIS2 law in force since 6 December 2025, with 4,739 manufacturing registrations; four Member States referred to the Court of Justice on 8 July 2026; UK Bill without Royal Assent.
Supply-chain duties of in-scope customers reach out-of-scope suppliers through contracts, and liability for software and missing security updates applies once national laws are in place.
Check that lending documentation reflects product-security reporting, liability exposure and customer-imposed cyber clauses; ask defence suppliers about certification status.
Not covered in source edition: supervisory priorities and consequences of non-compliance beyond fine maxima; national NIS2 extensions not surveyed; US items comparative only.

elements.visible_text: JLR booked GBP 196 million and GBP 64 million of cyber-related exceptional costs in two quarters, while free cash outflow reached GBP 791 million and GBP 1.5 billion with cyber and non-cyber causes.
Recovery tails outlast outages: JLR production was normal by mid-November 2025, but wholesales fell 43.3% in the following quarter; Asahi delayed its FY2025 results by five months.
Watch facility drawdown and receivables concentration after a major customer incident; JLR's undrawn bridge fell from GBP 2.0 billion to GBP 1.0 billion by 31 March 2026.
Values differ in currency, statistic type and population and are not summed. Not covered in source edition: five-year cost trend, sector business-interruption benchmarks and ransom data.

slides.label: Cyber-to-Credit Risk Transmission & Stress Scenarios
slides.headline: Illustrative - not a forecast or loss estimate: longer stops move the effect from delayed cash to working-capital drain and then to supplier liquidity and debt service.
bands: Duration not evidenced: legacy assumption of three to ten days; no multi-firm outage observed
Many plants stop on precaution while OT is untouched
Correlated delivery gaps; concurrent working-capital draws
Targeted disruption at a segmented manufacturer
Stryker restored manufacturing and ordering in about four weeks (Tier 1)
Production and shipping lost for weeks
Targeted disruption at a just-in-time OEM
JLR: about five weeks halted, normal production by mid-November, distribution later (Tier 1)
Supplier tiers idle; dealers lose volume
OEM cash outflow, emergency facilities, supplier prepayment, state guarantee
slides.band_note: Supply-chain concentration (scenario 3): mechanism kept, band duration not evidenced; the controller case was days old at the cut-off.

elements.visible_text: Transmission evidence: JLR's GBP 2 billion bridge facility, GBP 1.5 billion UKEF-guaranteed loan and supplier prepayment through a banking partner; the CMC modelled about GBP 108 million a week of JLR fixed cost and lost profit.
Duration and supplier dependence, not data loss, drive the cash-flow effect; buffered inventory, multi-sourcing and offline production release shorten it.
Borrower data needed: weeks of liquidity at zero output, revenue share of the largest customer, supply-chain finance use and insurance cover for customer-side disruption.
Illustrative: no probabilities and no loss estimates; the 1-week band and the supply-chain mechanism have no duration evidence in the source edition.

slides.label: Questionnaire-to-Sector Intelligence Mapping
slides.headline: Provisional map: seven generic discussion items link sector threats and incident evidence to credit consequences; no questionnaire was supplied, so no real item IDs are used.

rows: Plants stop -> revenue and cash loss
Can you release production and ship without ERP, MES and identity services for two weeks?
Do destructive administrative actions need a second approver?
Customer stop -> receivables and liquidity stress
What share of revenue comes from your largest customer, and how many weeks of stop could you finance?
Do you track internet exposure and end-of-support status of products you have sold?
Is provider remote access to OT restricted and logged?
How do you meet product vulnerability reporting that began in September 2026?
Uninsured loss -> margin and covenant pressure
Does your cyber cover include disruption at a key customer?

elements.visible_text: Derived from the source edition's seven actions (A1-A7) and five threat pathways (P1-P5); PROV IDs are placeholders, not questionnaire items.
Factors that change materiality: just-in-time versus buffered production, customer concentration, segmentation, installed-base size, defence or device regulation and liquidity headroom.
Borrower answers are self-reported, not confirmed evidence, and trigger no automatic adverse credit judgement.
Provisional: no questionnaire item list was supplied; the map must be rebuilt against actual item IDs.

slides.label: Credit Officer Engagement: Key Questions & Actions
slides.headline: Five client discussion topics, each with an early-warning indicator, let credit officers test continuity of production, supplier liquidity and debt service without assessing borrower controls.
topics: How long can you release production and ship without ERP, MES and identity services?
Which customer stop would stop you, and how would you bridge four weeks?
OEM incident notice; supplier short-time work
Who can wipe or reach every device and plant, and who approves it?
Government alert on administrative-tool misuse; disclosure citing an IT provider
How many of your connected units are online or out of support?
National CERT alert naming a product family
Is disruption at a key customer insured, and are reporting and liability duties met?
Insurer product change; first enforcement action
slides.referral: Specialist referral: involve cyber specialists when an indicator fires or answers show no tested fallback; record and monitor rather than change a rating.

elements.visible_text: Topics reframe the source edition's six challenge questions and five monitoring triggers for client discussion.
Practical improvements a client can make: documented manual release, second-approver controls, revenue diversification, exposure monitoring, restricted provider access and aligned cover.
Proportionate next steps: raise topics at review, record answers as self-reported and escalate to the Risk Committee when a trigger fires.
Topics are sector-informed priorities, not findings on any borrower's controls or creditworthiness.
